title: Former inhabitants
hookLine: he remembers those who lived in the woods before him, including formerly enslaved people (Walden 14)

cards: A dip in the ground in the woods, the size of a small room, softened by leaves. Stones at the edges. Nearby, a lilac bush, blooming among the trees, where no one would think to plant one.
To a hiker it's scenery. To Thoreau, walking the snowy woods around Walden, a hollow like that was a cellar hole, and a lilac by it meant a doorway once stood there. Someone lived here.
Someone planted that. So he stops admiring the wilderness long enough to ask who was here before him.

teach.b: First, the woods weren't empty. In the chapter Former Inhabitants, Thoreau walks the roads and hollows near his cabin and names the people who had lived there. Second, who they were.
Some had been enslaved. He tells of Cato Ingraham, enslaved by a Concord gentleman, who was given a house and leave to live in Walden Woods.
He tells of Zilpha, a Black woman who had a small house by the road, where she spun linen, and whose house was burned while she was away.
He tells of Brister Freeman, once enslaved, who planted apple trees, and of his wife Fenda, who told fortunes, Thoreau says, pleasantly.
A hill there is still known by Brister's name, and Thoreau says he read Brister's gravestone in an old burying ground. Third, the others.

teach.h: PEOPLE ON THE EDGE OF TOWN.
teach.b: He remembers poorer white neighbors too, a potter, and men who drank hard, people who lived on the edge of the town in every sense. The woods were where people went who had nowhere else. Fourth, why it matters.
Walden is read as a book about solitude and nature.

But here, late in the book, Thoreau stops to say that the wild place he loved was full of human stories, some of them hard, and that the lilacs were still blooming for people the town might easily have forgotten.
He doesn't fix that, and the chapter doesn't pretend to. He does something smaller and real.

how: Readers of Former Inhabitants often take it as a call to remember who lived in a place before them, including people who were enslaved or poor and are seldom remembered.

gather the names and stories of the people who lived there.
games.why: he wrote a whole chapter of names: Cato, Zilpha, Brister, Fenda, and the poor families who lived on the edge of town.

practice: Feel the ground under you, the floor, the building, the street, and ask quietly: who was here before me? The last people in this home, the people who built it, the people on this land before there were streets at all.
You may not know their names, and that's all right; hold the question with respect, the way you'd stand by a cellar hole in the woods, and if you pray, remember them in your own way.

wordCard.voice: Former inhabitants. Thoreau's chapter naming the people who lived in Walden Woods before him, among them Cato, Zilpha, Brister and Fenda. Today's word.

carryVoice: Your line: who was here. Every place holds names worth remembering. Back tomorrow, same hill.
